lead: A TRIAC and a DIAC together make a simple bidirectional AC switch. The TRIAC carries current in both half-cycles; the DIAC gives a clean trigger pulse at a set voltage. They appear in lamp dimmers, table-fan regulators and small AC motor controls. A GTO is different: it is a thyristor that a negative gate pulse can turn off, so it suits DC and high-power switching where an SCR would need extra commutation. The structures, V-I curves, triggering and limits follow.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for SCR latching and Chapter 1.3 for gate triggering.

blocks.text: A TRIAC is a three-terminal AC switch. Its terminals are main terminal 1 (MT1), main terminal 2 (MT2) and gate (G). It works like two SCRs connected in antiparallel between MT2 and MT1. Some syllabi call it a bidirectional triode thyristor.

In the positive half-cycle, MT2 is positive with respect to MT1. The upper SCR can turn on and current flows from MT2 to MT1. In the negative half-cycle, MT1 is positive, so the lower SCR turns on and current flows from MT1 to MT2. The gate near MT1 supplies trigger current to whichever SCR is forward biased.

The TRIAC latches like an SCR. After turn-on it stays on until the current falls below the holding current, which happens near the zero crossing in a 50 Hz supply. Its V-I curve therefore has forward and reverse blocking regions and conduction regions in both directions. One TRIAC replaces two SCRs in a lamp dimmer or a table-fan regulator.

Four triggering quadrants exist. A quadrant is set by two signs: the polarity of MT2 with respect to MT1, and the polarity of the gate with respect to MT1. In quadrant I, MT2 is positive and the gate is positive. In quadrant II, MT2 is positive and the gate is negative. In quadrant III, MT2 is negative and the gate is negative. In quadrant IV, MT2 is negative and the gate is positive.

A TRIAC is not equally sensitive in all four quadrants. Datasheets give the gate current needed in each quadrant; many designs use quadrants I and III, but the correct choice comes from the datasheet. A gate pulse with the wrong polarity may need more current or may fail to trigger.

A DIAC is a two-terminal bidirectional trigger diode. It has no gate. It blocks current in both directions until the voltage across it reaches the breakover voltage V<sub>BO</sub>, often about 30 V. Then it conducts and its voltage drops, so it delivers a sharp current pulse. In a simple lamp dimmer, an RC network charges until the DIAC reaches V<sub>BO</sub>, the DIAC fires, and the pulse triggers the TRIAC. The resistor sets the delay and so sets the firing angle.
The DIAC V-I curve is symmetric: it blocks up to +VBO and −VBO, then enters a negative-resistance conduction region. Gate drive details for TRIACs are in Chapter 1.7.

A GTO (gate turn-off thyristor) is a four-layer PNPN device like an SCR, but its gate and cathode are interdigitated. The gate therefore touches the whole cathode area and can pull stored charge out of the device. It turns on with a positive gate pulse, like an SCR. It turns off with a negative gate pulse, which an SCR cannot do.
The turn-off gain compares anode current to peak negative gate current.

blocks.where: β<sub>off</sub> is the turn-off gain (no unit); I<sub>A</sub> is the anode current just before turn-off in amperes; I<sub>G(off)</sub> is the peak negative gate current in amperes.

blocks.text: A GTO has a low β<sub>off</sub>, often only a few. A 100 A anode current with β<sub>off</sub> = 5 needs a 20 A negative gate pulse. That large pulse is the price of gate turn-off.

The GTO V-I curve is similar to the SCR curve in forward blocking and forward conduction. Many GTOs are asymmetric and have limited reverse blocking, so check the datasheet. GTOs were used in traction, large DC drives, HVDC and pulsed power. IGBTs and IGCTs have replaced them in many new designs. Gate drive circuits are covered in Chapter 1.7.

examples.question: A TRIAC phase controller runs from a 230 V rms, 50 Hz supply with a 100 Ω resistive load. The firing angle is α = 90°. Find the rms load voltage and the load power. Use V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> sqrt(1 − α/π + sin(2α)/(2π)).
steps: Write the data: V<sub>s</sub> = 230 V rms, f = 50 Hz, R = 100 Ω, and α = 90° = π/2 rad.
Compute α/π = (π/2)/π = 0.5. Also 2α = π, so sin(2α) = sin(π) = 0, and sin(2α)/(2π) = 0.
examples.answer: The rms load voltage is 162.6 V and the load power is 264.5 W.
examples.check:
import math
Vs = 230.0
alpha = math.pi / 2
R = 100.0
Vrms = Vs * math.sqrt(1 - alpha / math.pi + math.sin(2 * alpha) / (2 * math.pi))
P = Vrms ** 2 / R
print(round(Vrms, 1))
print(round(P, 1))

traps: Do not call MT1 and MT2 anode and cathode. Their roles swap every half-cycle; only the gate stays the control terminal.
A TRIAC is not equally sensitive in all four quadrants. A gate pulse with the wrong polarity may need more current or may fail to trigger; use the datasheet values.
A DIAC does not set the load power by itself. It only fires at V<sub>BO</sub>; the RC time constant sets the firing angle.
GTO turn-off is not a small gate signal. The turn-off gain is low, so the negative gate pulse can be a large fraction of the anode current.
With an inductive load, a TRIAC can fail to commutate at zero current because the voltage rises fast and retriggers it. A snubber or a different device may be needed.

quiz.q: Name the three terminals of a TRIAC and state how many SCRs it equivalently contains.
quiz.a: MT1, MT2 and gate; two SCRs in antiparallel.

quiz.q: Why can a TRIAC conduct in both half-cycles of an AC supply?
quiz.a: The two antiparallel SCR paths take turns: one conducts when MT2 is positive, the other when MT1 is positive; the gate triggers the forward-biased path.

quiz.q: A TRIAC feeds a 100 Ω resistor from 115 V rms with α = 90°. Find the load power. Use V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> sqrt(1 − α/π + sin(2α)/(2π)).
Why can a TRIAC fail to commutate with a highly inductive load?
quiz.a: Load current lags voltage. At zero current the voltage across the TRIAC is not zero and can rise fast. If dv/dt is high or the gate is still driven, the TRIAC can retrigger and stay on instead of turning off.
β<sub>off</sub> = I<sub>A</sub> / I<sub>G(off)</sub>, the anode current before turn-off divided by the peak negative gate current.

quiz.q: Compare how an SCR and a GTO turn off.
quiz.a: An SCR needs natural or forced commutation to reduce anode current below holding current; its gate cannot turn it off. A GTO turns off by a negative gate pulse that extracts stored charge; it needs a large gate current but no separate commutation circuit.

quiz.q: A GTO carries 100 A and has β<sub>off</sub> = 5. Find the peak negative gate current.

beyond: Not for the exam. TRIACs still sit inside millions of cheap lamp dimmers and fan regulators, often with a DIAC in the gate circuit. GTOs were common in traction and HVDC before IGBT and IGCT modules took over. Modern high-power converters often use IGCTs, which keep the thyristor-like low conduction loss but need a hard gate drive. Search for TRIAC quadrant triggering, GTO turn-off gain and IGCT versus GTO to go further.
